lessons.name: Analyze passages from Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry : Part 1

content.text: Read the following passage from Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry. In this excerpt, Cassie, the narrator, is walking to school with her brothers, Stacey and Little Man, and their friend T.J.

textContent.text: We were nearing the second crossroads, where deep gullies lined both sides of the road and the dense forest crept to the very edges of high, jagged, clay-walled banks. Suddenly, Stacey turned. "Quick!" he cried. "Off the road!" Without another word, all of us but Little Man scrambled up the steep right bank into the forest.
"Get up here, Man," Stacey ordered, but Little Man only gazed at the ragged red bank sparsely covered with scraggly brown briars and kept on walking. "Come on, do like I say."
"But I'll get my clothes dirty!" protested Little Man.
"You're gonna get them a whole lot dirtier you stay down there. Look!"

Little Man turned around and watched saucer-eyed as a bus bore down on him spewing clouds of red dust like a huge yellow dragon breathing fire. Little Man headed toward the bank, but it was too steep. He ran frantically along the road looking for a foothold and, finding one, hopped onto the bank, but not before the bus had sped past enveloping him in a scarlet haze while laughing white faces pressed against the bus windows.
Little Man shook a threatening fist into the thick air, then looked dismally down at himself.

"Well, ole Little Man done got his Sunday clothes dirty," T.J. laughed as we jumped down from the bank. Angry tears welled in Little Man's eyes but he quickly brushed them away before T.J. could see them.
<citation>From Mildred D. Taylor, Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry. Copyright 1976 by Mildred D. Taylor</citation>

content.text: Why doesn't Little Man want to get off the road?

choices.text: He wants to stay on the path with T.J.
He wants to keep his clothes clean.
He wants to get on the bus with the other kids.

content.text: A Place in History

elements.text: Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry is part of a genre called historical fiction, meaning that the book is set in the past. The story takes place in rural Mississippi in 1933, right in the middle of a period of worldwide economic downturn called the Great Depression.

During the Depression, which lasted from 1929 through 1939, over thirteen million Americans lost their jobs, which meant that about twenty-five percent of working-aged Americans were unemployed. However, the unemployment rate was much higher among African Americans, especially those living in communities of the American South.

contents.text: Getting off the road means Little Man would have to walk on the red clay bank and risk getting his clothes dirty. To avoid this risk, he continues walking along the road even though Stacey yells at him to move. So, the reason Little Man doesn't want to get off the road is because he wants to keep his clothes clean.

To escape from the bus coming up the road, Cassie, her brothers, and T.J. have to climb up the tall banks of dirt to get to the forest above.

textContent.text: We were nearing the second crossroads, where deep gullies lined both sides of the road and the dense forest crept to the very edges of high, jagged, clay-walled banks. Suddenly, Stacey turned. "Quick!" he cried. "Off the road!" Without another word, all of us but Little Man scrambled up the steep right bank into the forest.
"Get up here, Man," Stacey ordered, but Little Man only gazed at the ragged red bank sparsely covered with scraggly brown briars and kept on walking. "Come on, do like I say."
"But I'll get my clothes dirty!" protested Little Man.
"You're gonna get them a whole lot dirtier you stay down there. Look!"

content.text: Little Man turned around and watched saucer-eyed as a bus bore down on him spewing clouds of red dust like a huge yellow dragon breathing fire.

pieces.text: Little Man headed toward the bank, but it was too steep. He ran frantically along the road looking for a foothold and, finding one, hopped onto the bank, but not before the bus had sped past enveloping him in a scarlet haze while laughing white faces pressed against the bus windows.

textContent.text: Little Man shook a threatening fist into the thick air, then looked dismally down at himself.

"Well, ole Little Man done got his Sunday clothes dirty," T.J. laughed as we jumped down from the bank. Angry tears welled in Little Man's eyes but he quickly brushed them away before T.J. could see them.

contents.text: When people are scared, they often widen their eyes. This can make their eyes look larger, which is why the narrator compares Little Man's frightened eyes to round plates. textContent.text: On the far side of the lawn I spied Moe Turner speeding toward the seventh-grade-class building, and wondered at his energy. Moe was one of Stacey's friends. He lived on the Montier plantation, a three-and-a-half-hour walk from the school. Because of the distance, many children from the Montier plantation did not come to Great Faith after they had finished the four-year school near Smellings Creek. But there were some girls and boys like Moe who made the trek daily, leaving their homes while the sky was black and not returning until all was blackness again. I for one was certainly glad that I didn't live that far away. I don't think my feet would have wanted that badly for me to be educated.
<citation>From Mildred D. Taylor, Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry. Copyright 1976 by Mildred D. Taylor</citation>

content.text: Real World Inspiration

elements.text: Published in 1976, Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry is the first best-selling novel by author Mildred D. Taylor. The story is set in Mississippi during the 1930s. Taylor used her own family as inspiration for her writing. Coming from a family of storytellers, Taylor used actual events from her family's history to inspire the plot of Roll of Thunder, Hear my Cry.

There are many similarities between the lives of the Taylor family and the fictional Logan family in Roll of Thunder. Just like the Logans, Taylor's family owned land in Mississippi. Both the fictional Logan family and the real Taylor family cared deeply about their land. Taylor went so far as to sell the typewriter on which she wrote Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry in order to earn the money needed to save her family's land.

textContent.text: On the far side of the lawn I spied Moe Turner speeding toward the seventh-grade-class building, and wondered at his energy. Moe was one of Stacey's friends. He lived on the Montier plantation, a three-and-a-half-hour walk from the school. Because of the distance, many children from the Montier plantation did not come to Great Faith after they had finished the four-year school near Smellings Creek. But there were some girls and boys like Moe who made the trek daily, leaving their homes while the sky was black and not returning until all was blackness again. I for one was certainly glad that I didn't live that far away. I don't think my feet would have wanted that badly for me to be educated.

textContent.text: We were nearing the second crossroads, where deep gullies lined both sides of the road and the dense forest crept to the very edges of high, jagged, clay-walled banks. Suddenly, Stacey turned. "Quick!" he cried. "Off the road!" Without another word, all of us but Little Man scrambled up the steep right bank into the forest.
"Get up here, Man," Stacey ordered, but Little Man only gazed at the ragged red bank sparsely covered with scraggly brown briars and kept on walking. "Come on, do like I say."
"But I'll get my clothes dirty!" protested Little Man.
"You're gonna get them a whole lot dirtier you stay down there. Look!"

Little Man turned around and watched saucer-eyed as a bus bore down on him spewing clouds of red dust like a huge yellow dragon breathing fire. Little Man headed toward the bank, but it was too steep. He ran frantically along the road looking for a foothold and, finding one, hopped onto the bank, but not before the bus had sped past enveloping him in a scarlet haze while laughing white faces pressed against the bus windows.
Little Man shook a threatening fist into the thick air, then looked dismally down at himself.

"Well, ole Little Man done got his Sunday clothes dirty," T.J. laughed as we jumped down from the bank. Angry tears welled in Little Man's eyes but he quickly brushed them away before T.J. could see them.
<citation>From Mildred D. Taylor, Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry. Copyright 1976 by Mildred D. Taylor</citation>

content.text: A Place in History

elements.text: Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry is part of a genre called historical fiction, meaning that the book is set in the past. The story takes place in rural Mississippi in 1933, right in the middle of a period of worldwide economic downturn called the Great Depression.

During the Depression, which lasted from 1929 through 1939, over thirteen million Americans lost their jobs, which meant that about twenty-five percent of working-aged Americans were unemployed. However, the unemployment rate was much higher among African Americans, especially those living in communities of the American South.

textContent.text: We were nearing the second crossroads, where deep gullies lined both sides of the road and the dense forest crept to the very edges of high, jagged, clay-walled banks. Suddenly, Stacey turned. "Quick!" he cried. "Off the road!" Without another word, all of us but Little Man scrambled up the steep right bank into the forest.
"Get up here, Man," Stacey ordered, but Little Man only gazed at the ragged red bank sparsely covered with scraggly brown briars and kept on walking. "Come on, do like I say."
"But I'll get my clothes dirty!" protested Little Man.
"You're gonna get them a whole lot dirtier you stay down there. Look!"

content.text: Little Man turned around and watched saucer-eyed as a bus bore down on him spewing clouds of red dust like a huge yellow dragon breathing fire.

pieces.text: Little Man headed toward the bank, but it was too steep. He ran frantically along the road looking for a foothold and, finding one, hopped onto the bank, but not before the bus had sped past enveloping him in a scarlet haze while laughing white faces pressed against the bus windows.

textContent.text: Little Man shook a threatening fist into the thick air, then looked dismally down at himself.

"Well, ole Little Man done got his Sunday clothes dirty," T.J. laughed as we jumped down from the bank. Angry tears welled in Little Man's eyes but he quickly brushed them away before T.J. could see them.

textContent.text: On the far side of the lawn I spied Moe Turner speeding toward the seventh-grade-class building, and wondered at his energy. Moe was one of Stacey's friends. content.text: Real World Inspiration

elements.text: Published in 1976, Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry is the first best-selling novel by author Mildred D. Taylor. The story is set in Mississippi during the 1930s. Taylor used her own family as inspiration for her writing. Coming from a family of storytellers, Taylor used actual events from her family's history to inspire the plot of Roll of Thunder, Hear my Cry.

There are many similarities between the lives of the Taylor family and the fictional Logan family in Roll of Thunder. Just like the Logans, Taylor's family owned land in Mississippi. Both the fictional Logan family and the real Taylor family cared deeply about their land. Taylor went so far as to sell the typewriter on which she wrote Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry in order to earn the money needed to save her family's land.

textContent.text: On the far side of the lawn I spied Moe Turner speeding toward the seventh-grade-class building, and wondered at his energy. Moe was one of Stacey's friends. He lived on the Montier plantation, a three-and-a-half-hour walk from the school. Because of the distance, many children from the Montier plantation did not come to Great Faith after they had finished the four-year school near Smellings Creek. But there were some girls and boys like Moe who made the trek daily, leaving their homes while the sky was black and not returning until all was blackness again. I for one was certainly glad that I didn't live that far away. I don't think my feet would have wanted that badly for me to be educated.
<citation>From Mildred D. Taylor, Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry. Copyright 1976 by Mildred D. Taylor</citation>

textContent.text: We were nearing the second crossroads, where deep gullies lined both sides of the road and the dense forest crept to the very edges of high, jagged, clay-walled banks. Suddenly, Stacey turned. "Quick!" he cried. "Off the road!" Without another word, all of us but Little Man scrambled up the steep right bank into the forest.
"Get up here, Man," Stacey ordered, but Little Man only gazed at the ragged red bank sparsely covered with scraggly brown briars and kept on walking. "Come on, do like I say."
"But I'll get my clothes dirty!" protested Little Man.
"You're gonna get them a whole lot dirtier you stay down there. Look!"

Little Man turned around and watched saucer-eyed as a bus bore down on him spewing clouds of red dust like a huge yellow dragon breathing fire. Little Man headed toward the bank, but it was too steep. He ran frantically along the road looking for a foothold and, finding one, hopped onto the bank, but not before the bus had sped past enveloping him in a scarlet haze while laughing white faces pressed against the bus windows.
Little Man shook a threatening fist into the thick air, then looked dismally down at himself.

"Well, ole Little Man done got his Sunday clothes dirty," T.J. laughed as we jumped down from the bank. Angry tears welled in Little Man's eyes but he quickly brushed them away before T.J. could see them.
<citation>From Mildred D. Taylor, Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry. Copyright 1976 by Mildred D. Taylor</citation>

content.text: A Place in History

elements.text: Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry is part of a genre called historical fiction, meaning that the book is set in the past. The story takes place in rural Mississippi in 1933, right in the middle of a period of worldwide economic downturn called the Great Depression.

During the Depression, which lasted from 1929 through 1939, over thirteen million Americans lost their jobs, which meant that about twenty-five percent of working-aged Americans were unemployed. However, the unemployment rate was much higher among African Americans, especially those living in communities of the American South.

lessons.name: Use context to identify the meaning of a word

header.text: <instructions>Read the passage and then answer the question.</instructions>

contents.text: After Bobby Fischer learned to play chess, he said it was all he wanted to do. He started playing when he was six and was soon beating older players. At fourteen, he became the youngest person ever to win the United States Chess Championship. He won the World Chess Championship in 1972, becoming the first American-born world champion. Fischer's victories led to an increase in chess's popularity in the United States. They also made Fischer famous around the world. Fischer, though, did not seem to enjoy the fame. He stopped seeing his friends, choosing instead to live as a recluse. Fischer played very little chess in the decades that followed, but he did play one more famous match. On the twentieth anniversary of his World Championship victory, he played a rematch against Boris Spassky. Showing that he was still a champion, Fischer once again defeated Spassky and claimed a 3.6 million dollar prize.
What is the meaning of recluse as used in the passage?

choices.text: a person who competes in marathons
a person who lives alone and avoids other people
a person who helps those who need assistance

contents.text: If you don't know the meaning of a word, you can look for context clues. Context clues are nearby words and phrases that help you figure out the meaning of an unknown word.

header.text: Here are some examples:

sentences.text: Janet's dog punctured her ball with his teeth, causing it to go flat.
You can guess that punctured means "made a hole in."
She had a map, so she offered to be the trip's navigator.
You can guess that a navigator is someone who gives directions on a journey.
The guard closely monitored the building. He was on the lookout for anything that seemed out of place.
You can guess that monitored means "watched."

choices.text: a person who competes in marathons
a person who lives alone and avoids other people
a person who helps those who need assistance

After her arrival, Phillis was sold to the Wheatleys, a Boston family whose last name she took. Members of the family helped teach Phillis how to read and write. She became one of the first American women to do so as well.

contents.text: The United States court system has three main levels. The first is the District Court, where trials are initially held. This trial court's decision is final unless a party appeals to the Court of Appeal. The appeals court reviews decisions by the District Court and decides if any errors were made. The last level is the United States Supreme Court, which chooses carefully which cases to hear—usually, it selects cases that involve important issues. The Supreme Court may also take a case if something egregious happened in the lower courts. For example, the court might consider a case where someone was denied a fair trial. The Supreme Court hears less than one percent of the cases brought to it.

contents.text: Reflexive pronouns are pronouns that end in -self or -selves.

header.text: A reflexive pronoun is used to refer back to the subject of the sentence or clause in which it appears. It should agree with that subject.

sentences.text: We helped ourselves to some more soup.
The subject of the sentence is we, so use ourselves.
After the guests left, Amy made herself a cup of tea.
The subject of the clause in which the pronoun appears is Amy. Amy can be called she, so use herself.

header.text: A reflexive pronoun can only be used to refer to the subject of the sentence or clause in which it appears. To refer to someone else or something else, a personal pronoun, like me, you, him, her, it, us, or them, should be used instead.

sentences.text: Jake wrote a note for himself.
The reflexive pronoun, himself, refers back to the subject, Jake.
Jake wrote a note for him.
The personal pronoun, him, must refer to someone other than the subject, Jake.
